items.title: pREST _groupby function-expression SQL injection (incomplete fix of CVE-2025-58450)
items.description:
What the fix did and the gap

The v2.3.0 fix (commit e88dabb) routed the _select field through a strict new gate, sanitizeSelectField (postgres.go:947/1003/2097). The sibling _groupby path was left on the far weaker isSafeSQLExpression. adapters/postgres/postgres.go, GroupByClause (line 1946): a _groupby field that contains balanced parens takes the raw-SQL-expression branch (around lines 1999-2006), gated only by isSafeSQLExpression (line 2001, defined at 2043). That gate validates only the OUTERMOST function name against a 13-entry allowlist and uses a character allowlist that permits spaces, single quotes and parens. It blocks ;, --, /* , unbalanced parens and an outer pg_ prefix, but NOT a trailing UNION SELECT ..., a nested (SELECT ...) subquery, or an inne

items.title: go-guerrilla crashes on a bare XCLIENT command (7-byte slice off-by-one panic)
items.description:
The defect

Confirmed at HEAD. server.go: cmdXCLIENT = []byte("XCLIENT") is 7 bytes (line 78), so the dispatch match cmdXCLIENT.match(cmd) only guarantees len(input) >= 7. The handler then slices input[8:] (line 586):

 case sc.XClientOn && cmdXCLIENT.match(cmd):
 if toks := bytes.Split(input[8:], []byte{' '}); len(toks) > 0 { // line 586

A client sending the bare command XCLIENT (exactly 7 bytes) hits input[8:7] and panics runtime error: slice bounds out of range [8:7]. handleClient runs in the per-connection goroutine (server.go:391) which has no recover(); the only recover() calls are in the backend mail-processing workers (a different goroutine never reached during command parsing), so the unrecovered panic crashes the whole SMTP daemon.

items.description:
Impact

amqtt is vulnerable to a remote denial of service caused by improper MQTT topic-filter validation combined with catastrophic regular-expression backtracking.

A single client can freeze the entire broker by sending one specially crafted SUBSCRIBE packet followed by one PUBLISH packet.

1. add_subscription() validates the placement of the single-level wildcard + using substring checks for /+ and +/, rather than verifying that each /-delimited level containing + is exactly +. items.title: appium allows unauthenticated arbitrary file/directory deletion in @appium/storage-plugin
items.description:
Summary

The Appium storage plugin exposes an HTTP endpoint POST /storage/delete that takes a user-supplied name and deletes it from the server storage folder. The handler passes name straight into path.join(storageRoot, name) and then fs.rimraf() without any path sanitization. By sending a name containing ../ sequences, an unauthenticated remote client can escape the storage root and recursively delete arbitrary files and directories that the Appium process user can write, anywhere on the host filesystem.

The same plugin's *upload* path validates the name via fs.sanitizeName (requireValidItemOptions), but the *delete* path does not an asymmetry that makes the missing validation unambiguous.

items.title: Refitter: Unrestricted OpenAPI references permit build-host SSRF and file inclusion
items.description:
Summary

Refitter (the refitter dotnet tool, built on NJsonSchema for $ref resolution) fetches remote
http(s) URLs and reads local files (including absolute paths and ../ traversal outside the input
directory), inlining the referenced schema into the generated Refit interface/contracts. Running
refitter --output Out.cs on a spec whose $ref points at an attacker/internal URL or an
arbitrary local file yields SSRF, remote file inclusion, and local file inclusion. Verified on
Refitter 2.0.0.

Details

- $ref: http://attacker-or-internal/evil.json#/... -> build host fetches (SSRF) and inlines the
 remote schema (RFI); confirmed property REMOTE_REFIT_PROP.
- $ref: /abs/path.json#/... or ../../secret.json#/... -> out-of-tree local file read + inlined
 (LFI);

items.title: NLTK: StreamBackedCorpusView constructor os.stat leaks out-of-root file existence, size, and mtime bypassing pathsec ENFORCE
items.description:
Summary

StreamBackedCorpusView, a public API in nltk/corpus/reader/util.py, applies the pathsec sandbox to the file content it reads but not to the file metadata it probes in its constructor. When the view is created with a plain string fileid, __init__ calls os.stat(self._fileid).st_size with no pathsec validation, so an application that passes an attacker influenced path to the constructor discloses whether an arbitrary out of root file exists and, if it does, its exact byte size and modification time, even when nltk.pathsec.ENFORCE is True. This is the residual metadata channel left open by the fix for CVE-2026-63312 (GHSA-x5ph-mj9p-rfr8), which closed arbitrary content read on the same code path but did not bring the sibling os.stat under the sandbox.

items.title: Next.js: Cache poisoning of shared fallback shells in Cache Components via request-supplied placeholder route params
items.description:
Self-hosted Next.js applications served with next start and built with cacheComponents: true but without Partial Prefetching accept a request-supplied route param value as a prerender placeholder. One unauthenticated GET request can poison the fallback shell cache entry that a family of routes shares.

Such a route is served from a shell that keeps its never-prerenderable params as placeholders, so every value of those params shares one cache entry. A path segment equal to the percent-encoded, bracketed name of its own route param is treated as an unresolved placeholder, and only that param is deferred. A layout above it then renders its concrete value into the shell during the blocking render, and the result, including its HTTP status, is stored under the shared key.

endpoint is dispatched with no authentication, session token, or Origin check.

server's Kubernetes tools (including destructive/write tools) without credentials,

MCP library: github.com/mark3labs/mcp-go v0.57.0
Default mode: sse (SERVER_MODE default), default port 8080, bind 0.0.0.0

Root cause (static trace: handleSSE -> handleMessage -> tools/call)
- main.go L129: server.NewSSEServer(s) is created with no auth option and no

items.title: Flyto2 Core: http.paginate follows server-supplied next-page URLs (Link header / cursor) without SSRF revalidation
items.description:
Summary
http.paginate validates only the initial base_url, then follows server-supplied pagination targets (RFC 5988 Link: rel="next" headers, cursor/offset URLs) in a loop without revalidating each follow-up URL. An attacker's first-page response can point next at an internal address, causing a second-order SSRF whose internal body is aggregated into the returned items.

Root Cause
src/core/modules/atomic/http/paginate.py:495 validates base_url (first URL only). The pagination loop _paginate_link_header reads next_url via _parse_link_header (:203), sets url=next_url (:208), and calls session.request(method, url) (:196) with NO validate call in the loop (:186-208 has zero guard calls).

Summary

django-docutils before 0.30.0 rendered reStructuredText through Docutils without protected web-safe defaults. items.title: NATS Server allows unauthenticated memory exhaustion through incomplete MQTT CONNECT packets
items.description:
Background

NATS.io is a high performance open source pub-sub distributed communication technology, built for the cloud, on-premise, IoT and edge computing.

The NATS Server supports MQTT clients, including authentication and parsing of MQTT CONNECT packets.

Problem Description

An unauthenticated MQTT client could cause the server to retain large incomplete MQTT CONNECT packets before authentication completed.

The parser retained partial pre-authentication packet data while waiting for the advertised MQTT packet length to be completed. An attacker could therefore consume server memory until authentication timeouts closed the connections.

Affected Versions

Versions v2.14.2, v2.12.11 and below are vulnerable. The issue is fixed in v2.14.3 and v2.12.12.

items.description:
Summary

NLTK exposes a compile-time regular-expression denial of service in its regex-search helpers. When an application passes untrusted text as the search pattern to TokenSearcher.findall() / Text.findall(), or as the tokenizer pattern to RegexpTokenizer, the pattern is handed to the third-party regex engine, whose compilation cost is roughly quadratic in the number of capturing groups. A short pattern of the form () repeated many times (for example "()" * 25000, about 50 KB) forces tens of seconds of synchronous CPU work before any match begins. The wall-clock timeout that NLTK added to guard matching does not apply during compilation, so a single small request pins a CPU core, and repeated or concurrent requests exhaust all cores and deny service.

NATS.io is a high performance open source pub-sub distributed communication technology, built for the cloud, on-premise, IoT and edge computing.

The NATS Server can accept client connections over WebSocket and can also support MQTT over WebSocket when MQTT is configured.

A WebSocket listener could route requests for the MQTT-over-WebSocket path into MQTT handling even when MQTT was not configured.

On affected deployments, an unauthenticated client with access to the WebSocket listener could reach uninitialized MQTT state and crash the server process.

This affects deployments that enable WebSocket while leaving MQTT disabled. Deployments where MQTT is intentionally configured initialize the MQTT state and are not affected in the same way.

items.title: NLTK: AllowlistUnpickler does not deny numpy submodule-local file-I/O sinks
items.description:
Summary

nltk.picklesec.allowlisted_pickle_load keyed its denylist of dangerous globals by export name, so numpy's file-I/O callables that live in submodules and are not re-exported under __module__ == "numpy" were never matched. Under the broad allowed_modules=("numpy", "scipy", "sklearn") allowance that TransitionParser.parse(depgraphs, modelFile) granted for model files, a crafted protocol 4 pickle could name numpy.lib._npyio_impl.recfromtxt (arbitrary file read, result returned to the caller of allowlisted_pickle_load) or numpy.lib.format.open_memmap (attacker-chosen file create), and the REDUCE opcode invoked them during the load.

Affected

nltk >= 3.10.0 and <= 3.10.3 (the allowlisting unpickler and the TransitionParser model path); numpy must be installed.

items.title: eml_parser: Algorithmic-complexity DoS (O(n^4) regex backtracking) in Received-header parsing
items.description:
Summary

eml_parser.routing.parserouting() dynamically builds a regex from up to four greedy .* groups (from (?P.*)by (?P.*)with (?P.*)for (?P.*)) terminated by an escaped literal of the date extracted from a normalized copy of the Received header. Because the date literal comes from the normalized text but is searched in the original line, a crafted header can make the trailing literal unmatchable; the search then fails at every start position only after exhaustively backtracking the four nested greedy groups — O(n^4) in header length. A single ~5.9 KB email pins one CPU core for ~12 seconds; doubling the input multiplies the cost ~25x, so a ~13 KB header takes minutes and a ~25 KB header effectively hangs the parse worker.

items.description:
Summary

NLTK's XMLCorpusView.read_block rebuilds the full root-to-node context path with "/".join(context) on every start tag while it is still searching for a matching element. Because the context stack grows with XML nesting depth and the join is repeated once per start tag, a single corpus file containing deeply nested tags forces O(n^2) pure-Python work, where n is the number of nested elements. SeekableUnicodeStreamReader.readline in nltk/data.py assembles a line by repeatedly reading a block, appending it to a growing chars buffer, and recomputing chars.splitlines(True) over the entire buffer on every loop iteration. The read block size doubles only until it caps at 8000 characters, so for a single unterminated line of N characters the loop runs about N/8000 iterations and iteration k re-scans roughly 8000*k characters, giving O(N^2) total work. items.title: fzf: Predictable FIFO path in zsh completion allows local symlink attack / arbitrary file overwrite as the victim user (_fzf_feed_fifo)
items.description:
Summary

shell/completion.zsh feeds every trigger-driven zsh completion through a FIFO at a predictable, PID-based path in shared /tmp (fzf-complete-fifo-$$), without checking the failure of rm -f/mkfifo. On a multi-user host, another local user can pre-create that path as a symlink to a victim-writable file (e.g. ~/.bashrc), causing the victim's own completion to overwrite it with the completion stream — with attacker-influenced content (e.g. via process names in ps output), escalating to code execution at the victim's next login. A pre-created plain FIFO instead leaks/blocks on the completion stream.

items.title: snark-verifier: Halo 2 aggregation circuit mishandles point-at-infinity proof elements
items.description:
Summary
The Halo 2 aggregation circuit could mishandle proof elements encoded as the point at infinity.

When an assigned proof point appeared in an MSM term with constant scalar one, the Halo 2 loader used a scalar-one shortcut that passed the assigned point directly into the EC sum helper. The EC sum implementation used by that path assumed its inputs were non-identity points, while assigned proof points could represent the encoded identity (0, 0).

Details
EcPointLoader::multi_scalar_multiplication partitions MSM terms by scalar and base type. For (Value::Constant(ONE), Value::Assigned(_)), the loader placed the assigned base into the non-scaled variable-base list and later passed those points to sum_with_const.

The default Halo 2 shim delegates sum_with_const to halo

items.title: Next.js: Cross-client response injection and disclosure in self-hosted Next.js applications forwarding fetched responses
items.description: Self-hosted Next.js applications (App Router route handlers and the fetch cache) that return a fetched upstream response unchanged can emit a response whose declared framing does not match the body actually sent. When such an application sits behind an HTTP/1.1 reverse proxy that permits pipelined response queueing, a crafted upstream response can desynchronize responses between clients, enabling response injection and disclosure of other clients' responses.

items.title: Jane: $ref resolution performs SSRF + LFI (path traversal) at code-generation time (jane-php)
items.description:
Summary
jane-php resolves external $ref targets at code-generation time via file_get_contents($ref) (jane-php/json-schema-runtime/Reference.php::doResolve) with no scheme/path restriction. An attacker-controlled OpenAPI document can therefore cause: $ref: 'http://attacker/x' -> SSRF (HTTP GET at gen time; response inlined = RFI); $ref: '/abs/file' -> LFI; $ref: '../secret.yaml' -> path-traversal LFI (CWE-22, arbitrary local JSON/YAML read). Verified 7.11.2/PHP8.1 (listener records the fetch; remote + ../ local content inlined into the generated code). file:// rejected. CWE-918/CWE-98/CWE-611/CWE-22.

Details
// Reference.php::doResolve()
$contents = file_get_contents($fragment); // $fragment = attacker-controlled $ref URI

items.title: Jupyter MCP Server: Browser DNS rebinding can hijack the Jupyter backend through management routes
items.description:
Standalone streamable-http mode in datalayer/jupyter-mcp-server rejects forged Host and Origin headers on /mcp, but custom management routes mounted on the same application do not get the same browser-origin protection. A malicious website can keep an attacker origin while its hostname resolves to 127.0.0.1 or a private target address, then send PUT /api/connect to replace the MCP server's active Jupyter backend. The route accepts the browser-shaped request and makes the server start a kernel client against attacker-controlled infrastructure.

The protected /mcp endpoint shows the intended browser-origin boundary. With MCP_TOKEN configured, /mcp rejects forged browser headers:

Host: attacker.example:8142

items.title: Guard Core: Whitespace-collapse preprocessing permanently disables the CRLF-anchored http-splitting and command-injection detectors in the default detection mode
items.description:
Summary

In the default "enhanced" detection mode, ContentPreprocessor.preprocess() collapses all whitespace (re.sub(r"\s+", " ", content), guard_core/detection_engine/preprocessor.py:137 on master 08780f1; :384 in the 3.12.0 sdist) before pattern matching. This erases every \r and \n from the scanned value, rendering two built-in detectors structurally unmatchable regardless of input:

- http_split — guard_core/handlers/suspatterns_handler.py:540: r"[\r\n]\s*(?:HTTP\/[0-9.]+|Location:|Set-Cookie:)" requires a literal \r or \n, which no longer exists after preprocessing;
- cmd_injection — r"\n\s*(?:bash|sh|...)\s+-c\b" — same structural death.

The downstream application receives the raw value with CRLF intact (Starlette percent-decodes %0d%0a in query

items.title: OliveTin: Second-Order OS Command Injection via shellAfterCompleted
items.description:
Summary

OliveTin's shellAfterCompleted post-execution hook injects unsanitized variables — including arbitrary command output (output), the authenticated username (ot_username), and the exit code (exitCode) — directly into a shell command template processed by sh -c. Unlike the main action's argument handling, no checkShellArgumentSafety validation is applied to these variables. An attacker who can influence the output of a command (e.g., via user-supplied arguments that reflect in stdout, or through trusted-header username spoofing) can inject arbitrary OS commands into the post-execution shell.

This is a distinct finding from CVE-2026-27626 (OS command injection via password type in webhooks). That CVE addressed argument types bypassing shell safety checks in t

items.title: Nuxt payload URL generation has quadratic cost for repeated slashes in the request path
items.description:
Summary

Nuxt strips trailing slashes from the request path with a regular expression whose cost grows quadratically with the length of a run of consecutive slashes. A single unauthenticated request with a long run of slashes can occupy the server's event loop for a noticeable time, delaying every other request handled by the same process.

Impact

When a page is rendered with payload extraction (any route covered by an isr, swr or cache route rule), Nuxt builds the _payload.json URL from the raw request path. A path such as /blog/a followed by 16,000 slashes and x, which fits within Node's default header size limit, takes roughly 0.1 to 0.4 seconds of synchronous CPU time per request, depending on hardware. items.title: AIOHTTP: Pure-Python parser request replay and buffer growth behind a declined upgrade
items.description:
Summary

When the pipelined request queue was full, the pure-Python parser stored the unparsed remainder internally and also returned it to the caller. After a handler declined an upgrade request, the buffered data was re-fed, so the buffer grew with each handled request and already-handled requests were dispatched to the application again.

Impact

If users are using the Python parser (AIOHTTP_NO_EXTENSIONS, or not a standard wheel installed), an attacker could cause excessive memory use and cause pipelined requests to be processed more than once.

Workaround

Switch to the default C parser.

Patch: https://github.com/aio-libs/aiohttp/commit/47babd8c23ca79e2bae6cc8dcb5752b61e369fc7

items.title: AIOHTTP: Concatenated compressed streams cause excessive CPU use
items.description:
Summary

When decompressing a payload made up of many concatenated compressed members (gzip, deflate or zstd), each member was decoded by passing the entire remaining input to a new decompressor, resulting in quadratic CPU time. Empty members produce no output, so client_max_size and output backpressure did not limit the work.

Impact

An attacker could block the event loop of a server with a specially crafted compressed request body or WebSocket message. A malicious server could do the same to a client.

Patch: https://github.com/aio-libs/aiohttp/commit/d925a80539ffd227da1d93ab4a5bff123cc777db

items.title: AIOHTTP: WebSocket max_msg_size bypass via integer overflow
items.description:
Summary

The max_msg_size check in the WebSocket reader added the declared frame length to the size of the partial message already buffered. In the C extension this addition is 64-bit arithmetic, so a declared length close to 2**63 overflowed and the check passed.

Impact

An attacker could bypass max_msg_size and cause unbounded memory use by streaming an oversized WebSocket message after a small non-final fragment.

Workaround

If unable to upgrade, the Python reader is unaffected and can be used with AIOHTTP_NO_EXTENSIONS=1.

Patch: https://github.com/aio-libs/aiohttp/commit/8cfbe9abe5e11b84006a10f9bdf82bf607671dab

items.title: AIOHTTP: Base64 multipart parts bypass client_max_size
items.description:
Summary

When reading a multipart part with Content-Transfer-Encoding: base64, BodyPartReader.read_chunk() kept reading until the chunk length was a multiple of 4, with no byte limit. A part with a short Content-Length, or a long run of whitespace, could cause the entire remaining body to be read into memory within a single call before any size check, or spin on the event loop.

Impact

An attacker could bypass client_max_size to cause excessive memory use, or block the event loop, with a specially crafted multipart request to any handler that reads multipart data.

Patch: https://github.com/aio-libs/aiohttp/commit/a555ab698e08e9baea7386d5b4c0761cb8956fdd

  src_dir = Path(info.get("source", ...)).parent

items.title: NLTK: Symlink escape in chat80.sql_query bypasses the pathsec data-root sandbox to read out-of-root SQLite databases
items.description:
Summary

nltk.sem.chat80.sql_query() opens a SQLite database by handing the result of nltk.data.find(dbname) straight to sqlite3.connect() without the path-containment check that the NLTK data sandbox (nltk.pathsec) is meant to enforce. nltk.data.find() applies only lexical checks to the resource name and returns a FileSystemPathPointer whose path is normalized with os.path.abspath but never resolved for symlinks. As a result, an in-root symbolic link that points at a SQLite file outside every registered NLTK data root is followed by SQLite, and the caller receives query results from the out-of-sandbox database. items.title: mail-parser: Path Traversal vulnerability in attachment extraction
items.description:
A path traversal vulnerability was identified in mail-parser when extracting email attachments using the write_attachments() and write_sample() APIs.

A specially crafted email containing malicious attachment filenames (for example, using directory traversal sequences such as "../" or absolute filesystem paths) could cause files to be written outside the intended output directory. Depending on how the library was used and the permissions of the executing process, this could result in arbitrary file overwrite.

The vulnerability affects mail-parser versions 3.8.0 through 4.5.0.

The issue has been addressed by introducing comprehensive filename sanitization and path validation before any file is written to disk. The fix includes:

- Sanitization of attachment filenames before writing.

items.description:
Summary

Nuxt matches route rules against the request path with encoded slashes (%2F) left encoded, while the page router decodes them into route params. A request that spells a slash as %2F can therefore render a page through a catch-all route without the route rules configured for the path it resolves to. The fix for GHSA-6gq8-jgmh-3ffp (https://github.com/nuxt/nuxt/security/advisories/GHSA-6gq8-jgmh-3ffp) deliberately left reserved escapes such as %2F encoded, so it did not cover this form.

Impact

An unauthenticated attacker can bypass route rules that protect paths served by a catch-all page route, or by a custom route whose param can span several segments.

items.title: mail-parser: Uncaught OverflowError / OSError on an out-of-range Received date
items.description:
Impact

A Received header whose trailing date carries an out-of-range year, or a timezone offset
large enough to push the timestamp past the int64 epoch range, raises an exception that is
outside the MailParser* hierarchy. A caller that catches only mail-parser exceptions
does not catch it, and the parse of the entire message is aborted — the same class of issue
as GHSA-24mq-4vc6-2prf (https://github.com/SpamScope/mail-parser/security/advisories/GHSA-24mq-4vc6-2prf),
which this survives (it is not a duplicate; 24mq is fixed in 4.6.2 and this reproduces on 4.6.2).

All entry points are affected: parse_from_string(), parse_from_bytes(), parse_from_file(),
parse_from_file_obj() and the mail-parser CLI. The header is fully attacker-controlled and
a single line is enough,

items.title: Nuxt exposes the message and data of unhandled errors thrown during server rendering
items.description:
Summary

When a page, plugin or route middleware throws an error that is not an HTTP error, Nuxt wraps it with createError before rendering the error page. The wrapped error was treated as one the app raised deliberately, so in production its message and data were sent to the client in the error page payload (__NUXT_DATA__) and in JSON error responses. For a failed $fetch, that is the URL that was requested (including its query string) and the body of the upstream error response.

Impact

An application is affected if server-rendered code lets an error with sensitive details reach the error page, for example:

items.title: NLTK: Path Traversal in save_maxent_params / load_maxent_params Allow Arbitrary File READ/WRITE
items.description:
Summary
Path traversal in NLTK's save_maxent_params() and load_maxent_params() allows arbitrary file write and arbitrary file read outside the directories permitted by NLTK's pathsec security mechanism.

This vulnerability was previously reported through Huntr, accepted by the NLTK project, and assigned CVE-2026-15367. A $750 bounty was paid through Huntr (i didnt get the fix bounty). Huntr subsequently shut down its OSS vulnerability program, so I am submitting this report through GitHub to continue the existing disclosure process and preserve the original CVE assignment and researcher credit.

Details
The affected functions are:

- nltk.classify.maxent.load_maxent_params()
- nltk.classify.maxent.save_maxent_params()

Both functions construct filesystem paths from the caller-contr

items.description:

Patch: https://github.com/aio-libs/aiohttp/commit/3d850ee9b92573c7e913821cbcb96005beb3f4df

items.title: AIOHTTP: Event loop stall in add_domain() wildcard matching
items.description:
Summary

Application.add_domain() compiled each * in a host mask to [^:]*. With two or more wildcards in a mask, matching a long Host header that does not match the mask took polynomial time on the event loop.

Impact

An attacker could stall a server that registers a domain mask with more than one wildcard by sending requests with a long Host header.

Workaround

Use at most one * in a domain mask.

Patch: https://github.com/aio-libs/aiohttp/commit/c6ac0e44c3c573ff9616f4a6a532992538b31e43

items.title: AIOHTTP: WebSocket receive queue limits bypassed by small or compressed messages
items.description:
Summary

The WebSocket reader continued parsing frames already received after the receive queue had paused the transport, and empty messages were not counted towards the queue size. With permessage-deflate, a single read of compressed frames could add many megabytes of decompressed messages to the queue.

Impact

An attacker could cause excessive memory use in a WebSocket server, or a malicious server against a client, by sending many small or compressed messages faster than the application consumes them.

Patch: https://github.com/aio-libs/aiohttp/commit/0ae507423f681161efa77d20052b4054397c7fb6
